title: Startrails above VISTA
caption: Star trails above the VISTA telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: Star trails fill a cloudy sky above ESO's VISTA telescope. Its full name is the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, and it is part of ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile.

The trails appear because the photograph gathers light over a long period while Earth rotates, so each star is stretched into an arc. The clouds add a softer texture and show that even the best sites do not have perfectly clear skies every night.

VISTA has a particular job. It works at near-infrared wavelengths, just beyond the red end of what our eyes can see, and ESO describes it as the largest survey telescope in the world. A survey telescope is designed to map large areas of sky systematically rather than study one object in fine detail, building up catalogues that other telescopes can follow up.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at Paranal. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points. The long exposure turns them into trails. VISTA itself works in near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

explore: Infrared light can pass through dust that blocks visible light, which is one reason near-infrared surveys are useful for studying crowded, dusty regions of the sky. VISTA is built for exactly this.
alt: Star trails across a cloudy night sky above a telescope enclosure.
